nodes.question: How does diversification benefit intensively managed cropping systems according to the paragraph?
nodes.answer: Diversification enhances productivity, resource use efficiency, soil health, and economic returns while reducing the carbon footprint of intensively managed cropping systems.

Both sites were equipped with an on-site weather station for precipitation and tem- perature measurements. The 30-year climate normal data were retrieved from Environment Canada weather stations. At Swift Current, average annual precipitation during the 8-year study period was 401 mm (Table S1), higher than the 1991 2020 climate normal of 394 mm (ECCC 2024), with 250 mm occurring during the typical growing season (May to August). At Brooks, annual precipitation averaged from 2011 to 2018 was 288 mm, slightly below the 1991 2020 climate normal of 299 mm (ECCC 2024), with 177 mm occurring from May to August (Table S1). nodes.question: What role do pulse crops play in crop diversification?
nodes.answer: Crop diversification, especially with pulse crops, often leads to nitrogen fertility improvement.
nodes.paragraph: 17 (Degani et al. 2019; Gaudin et al. 2015; Lin 2011; Reck - ling et al. 2022), and provide yield benefits under various growing conditions (Angus et al. 2015; Bowles et al. 2020; Jarecki et al. 2018). Diversifying cropping systems can enhance resilience by suppressing pests, improving soil fertility, and enhancing beneficial soil biota (Bennett et al. 2012; Linton et al. 2020; McDaniel et al. 2014; Tiemann et al. 2015; Tilman et al. 2014), while also attenuating the adverse effects caused by variable weather (Roesch-McNally et al. 2018). Conversely, simplified cropping systems may degrade soil quality due to losses in soil organic carbon and N (Bardgett and van der Putten 2014). Crop diversification, especially with pulse crops, often leads to N fertility improvement (Lin 2011; Ochieng et al. 2020). The study by Sanford et al. (2021) suggested that the enhanced resilience of diversified crop - ping systems may be linked to gradual improvements in soil health over time.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Sustainable agricultural practices|Crop diversification_qna_002
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What geographical area is the study conducted in?
nodes.answer: The study is conducted in the Mixed Grassland Ecoregion of Canada, specifically at the Crop Diversification Centre in Brooks and Swift Current, Alberta.
nodes.paragraph: The same study was repeated from 2011 to 2018 at the Crop Diversification Centre, Brooks (50 33 N; 111 53 W; elevation: 747m), Alberta, Canada. Both sites are located in the Mixed Grassland Ecoregion of Canada, in an area where Brown Chernozem soils are prevalent. The soil (0 15 cm) at Swift Current is a silt loam, with 31% sand, 51% silt, and 18% clay, whereas at Brooks the soil (0 15 cm) is a sandy loam, with 46% sand, 32% silt, and 22% clay. At the initiation of this study, soil in the 0 15 cm layer at the Swift Current site had a pH (1:2 ratio of soil to water) of 6.5, bulk density of 1.3 g cm 3, organic carbon (dry combustion after removing inorganic using 6 M HCI) of 10.6 g kg 1, mineral N (2 M KCI extractable N) of 3.4 mg kg 1, and Olsen P (0.5 M NaHCO3) of 26.5 mg kg 1.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Sustainable agricultural practices|Crop diversification_qna_003
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What was the impact of diversifying cropping systems with pulse crops on soil organic carbon?
nodes.answer: Diversifying cropping systems with pulse crops had no adverse effect on soil organic carbon, despite relatively low straw returns from pulse crops.
nodes.paragraph: There was no difference between moderately and highly diversified rotations, suggesting that a large portion of diversification benefits can be achieved at the moderately diversified rotation level. Compared with the wheat monocrop, diversified rotations reduced nitrogen fertilizer inputs and resulted in a 10 31% lower partial nitrogen balance at the end of 8-year rotations. Moreover, diversifying cropping systems with pulse crops had no adverse effect on soil organic carbon, despite relatively low straw returns from pulse crops. These results, assessed using multiple system indicators at both the crop phase and rotation levels, reveal that diversifying rotations with pulse crops, even at a moderate level, can effectively improve the ecosystem services, contributing to the sustainability of cropping systems. Keywords Cropping system Integrated assessment Systems approach Diversification 1 Introduction Growing crops in short rotations is a global trend in inten- sively managed conventional cropping systems (Bennett et al. 2012; Marini et al. 2020). According to Benbi (2018), high agrochemical inputs in simplified cropping systems resulted in a ~2.5-fold increase in yields but a 3-fold increase in greenhouse gas emission.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Sustainable consumption and production|Sustainable agricultural practices|Crop diversification_qna_004
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: How has diversification of cropping systems impacted yield trends according to Bennett et al. (2012)?
nodes.answer: Diversification of cropping systems has proven effective in reversing the declining yield trends.
nodes.paragraph: Yields often show a declining trend in short and simplified crop rotations, as reported by Hooper et al. (2012), who found a yield reduction of 5 10% in response to a 21 40% decrease in crop species. Diversification of cropping systems has proven effective in reversing this declining trend (Bennett et al. 2012). Yields tend to increase with greater diversity, although the posi- tive effect might not always be significant (Archer et al. 2020). nodes.question: What benefits do diversified cropping systems provide?
nodes.answer: Diversified cropping systems enhance ecosystem services, particularly in pest control and nutrient cycling, thereby reducing reliance on external inputs and benefiting farmers while delivering public goods to society.
nodes.paragraph: As a result, researchers advocate for crop diversification to adapt to climate change and enhance crop- ping system resilience to biotic and abiotic stresses (Degani et al. 2019; Gaudin et al. 2015; Lin 2011; Ratnadass et al. 2021; Sanford et al. 2021 ), thus reducing yield loss risk under unfavorable growing conditions. Crop diversity influences a variety of ecosystem pro- cesses, including primary productivity, pest suppression, nutrient cycling, and soil organic matter dynamics. Diversi- fied cropping systems enhance ecosystem services, particu- larly in pest control and nutrient cycling, thereby reducing reliance on external inputs, offering benefits to farmers, and delivering public goods to society (Isbell et al. 2017; Smith et al. 2008). With the increasing demand for ecosystem ser - vices in cropping systems, diversification with suitable crop species could be essential for sustaining yield and ecosystem services in dominant cropping systems. nodes.question: What hypothesis was tested regarding highly diversified cropping systems?
nodes.answer: The hypothesis was that highly diversified cropping systems would result in better overall system performance, as quantified by multiple ecosystem service indicators.
nodes.paragraph: Wheat and pulse crops are dominant crops in the semi-arid Cana- dian prairie region, where Liu et al. (2020) reported effects of various pulse crops on productivity and soil organic car - bon in pulse-wheat cropping systems, but did not address Diversifying wheat -based cropping systems with pulse crops enhances ecosystem services 17 the impact of crop diversification with pulse crops on the overall performance of cropping systems. Further diversify - ing wheat-pulse cropping systems is considered a promising strategy to enhance the sustainability of cropping systems in this semi-arid region. The objective of this study was to assess the overall performance of cropping systems with different levels of diversification during an 8-year study period using multiple indicators collectively in the semi- arid Canadian prairies.
